summary.central_question: If the US imposes the full threatened tariffs, will China hold the yuan stable or let it weaken to offset the trade hit?
summary.main_thesis: China can choose either path, but it will most likely limit near-term depreciation while it tests whether a deal is still possible.

content.text: If the US imposes the full threatened tariffs, will China hold the yuan stable or let it weaken to offset the trade hit?
content.reason: A country hit by a large external trade shock must choose whether to absorb it or shift it through the exchange rate.

passages.source_excerpt: Will China continue to want to keep its currency stable, or would it want to try to offset the (substantial) trade impact of “full” U.S. tariffs with a weaker yuan?

content.text: Signals had pointed to a modest US-China deal: Trump's tweets, early soybean purchases, summit preparations and a stable yuan, but the deal collapsed within a week.
content.reason: When convergent signals of an agreement are suddenly reversed, the shift calls for re-examining each side's options.

passages.source_excerpt: Until this past week, it looked like the United States and China were heading toward a deal. Not a great deal, but a deal.

content.text: Full 25 percent tariffs on about $550 billion of imports would raise $100 to 140 billion, a fiscal tightening of about half a point of GDP.
content.reason: Tariff revenue acts as a tax increase that withdraws demand from the economy.

passages.source_excerpt: Realistically, it might be more like $100 billion in new tariff revenue, given opportunities to substitute away from Chinese goods in some sectors—but that’s still a half point of GDP fiscal consolidation

content.text: The tariff drag is noticeable but too small to cause a US recession on its own, and it is far smaller than the drag from the 2014-15 dollar appreciation.
content.reason: Exchange rate swings can affect growth more than headline trade policy measures.

passages.source_excerpt: That’s big enough to notice but, as Dr. Krugman notes, not big enough to generate a recession on its own.

content.text: UBS estimates full tariffs plus retaliation could cut China's growth by 1.5 points, with exports to the US at about 3-4 percent of China's GDP.
content.reason: The size of a trade shock depends on the targeted exports' share of value added in output.

passages.source_excerpt: UBS estimates that 25 percent tariffs on all of China’s exports to the United States, plus Chinese retaliation against U.S. imports, might knock 1.5 percentage points off China’s GDP growth

content.text: Of China's retaliation options (soybeans, broader tariffs, squeezing GM, Airbus orders), letting the yuan weaken is the logical asymmetric response.
content.reason: A country facing tariffs can offset them through currency depreciation rather than matching tariff for tariff.

passages.source_excerpt: But letting the yuan weaken has always been, in my view, the logical “asymmetric” Chinese response to a trade war.

content.text: China has enough dollars at the central bank and in state banks to manage its currency, and fears about its foreign debt are overstated.
content.reason: A state holding ample foreign assets across its official and state-bank balance sheets can defend or steer its exchange rate.

passages.source_excerpt: In my view, China has the firepower it needs to continue to manage its currency (concerns about China’s foreign currency debts are overstated in aggregate

content.text: Critics overstated the problems with China's reported currency-stability commitment, since stability is already China's policy.
content.reason: A commitment that codifies existing policy imposes little additional cost.

passages.source_excerpt: Indeed, I thought much of the criticism of China’s reported commitment to currency stability in the (now aborted?) trade deal was overdone.

content.text: An even larger Chinese manufacturing surplus, already around $1 trillion, would harm the global economy and fuel populism in deindustrialized regions.
content.reason: Large manufacturing surpluses in a major economy displace production elsewhere and generate political backlash.

passages.source_excerpt: I for one don’t think an even larger Chinese manufacturing surplus would improve the global economy. It would also fan populist pressure

content.text: Tracking only official reserves misses China's real balance-of-payments flows, which now run through state bank lending and borrowing.
content.reason: Where state banks hold foreign assets, official reserves understate official external activity.

passages.source_excerpt: But looking only at reserves misses the real action in China’s balance of payments these days.

content.text: Chinese bank lending abroad has soared, funded by bank borrowing and $150-200 billion a year of portfolio inflows, and BIS data broadly agree with China's own data.
content.reason: Outflows must be financed by inflows or reserve drawdowns.

passages.source_excerpt: Every indicator I have found suggests the state banks now have a substantial (and growing) net foreign asset position.

content.text: Cross-checking China's bank data against BIS counterpart data supports its reliability.
content.reason: Counterparty data from an independent source can validate a country's self-reported figures.

passages.source_excerpt: The BIS data (which shows global banks exposure to China) isn’t that different from China’s own data.

content.text: The trade surplus covers tourism and errors while bank outflows match inflows, so the balance of payments roughly balances.
content.reason: The current account, financial flows and reserve changes must sum to zero.

passages.source_excerpt: China’s trade surplus, while reduced, is still sufficient to cover China’s tourism imports and the “error” term in the balance of payments. Everything, more or less, balanced.

content.text: Intervention proxies show state bank purchases and sales alternating, with no sustained pressure in either direction.
content.reason: Two-way intervention indicates a currency near its equilibrium under current controls.

passages.source_excerpt: There have been months when China’s state banks have sold foreign currency, but also months when China’s state banks have bought.

content.text: A stable yuan would keep China's balance of payments stable.
content.reason: Exchange rate expectations drive capital flows, so a credible stable rate keeps flows balanced.

passages.source_excerpt: as long as China’s currency stayed stable, its balance of payments, in my view, also would remain stable.

content.text: The recent history supports two readings: China need not upset its stability, or China is in enough control to engineer a weaker yuan.
content.reason: The same evidence of control can justify either preserving the status quo or using that control to change it.

passages.source_excerpt: One view, more or less, is that China has no need to upset the apple cart.

content.text: Even if tariffs and oil sanctions pushed China's current account into a modest deficit, a credible stability signal would keep portfolio inflows coming and protect reserves.
content.reason: Signaled currency stability sustains portfolio inflows that can finance a small external deficit.

passages.source_excerpt: if China signaled that the yuan would remain stable, portfolio inflows would likely continue—and a modest deficit need not put any real strain on China’s reserves

content.text: Controlled depreciation is hard because markets front-run predictable moves, but China could manage it by signaling a new floor and resetting the trading band.
content.reason: Anticipated depreciation invites speculative outflows unless authorities credibly cap the move.

passages.source_excerpt: Controlled depreciations are hard—the market (even a controlled market like the market for the yuan) obviously has an incentive to front run any predictable move (as China learned in 15 and 16).

content.text: A weaker yuan lets Chinese exporters cut dollar prices to offset tariffs and shift sales to other markets.
content.reason: Depreciation lowers foreign-currency prices while preserving domestic-currency revenue.

passages.source_excerpt: That would let Chinese firms (who have already started to complain) cut their dollar prices (offsetting some of the impact of the tariff) without reducing their yuan revenues

content.text: A weaker yuan would spread China's trade pain globally: other Asian currencies would follow, oil-importing emerging economies would face pressure, and European and Japanese exporters would lose.
content.reason: A large exporter's depreciation pushes competitors to follow and hurts export-reliant economies.

passages.source_excerpt: A weaker yuan, in effect, redistributes some of China’s trade pain globally, and thus poses a challenge to those parts of the world that have relied on exports

content.text: Depreciation could provoke Trump into higher or broader tariffs, so a major move is better timed after the tariffs are fully extended.
content.reason: A retaliatory move that invites counter-escalation is best saved until the opponent has used up its threats.

passages.source_excerpt: Oh, and Trump would also have to decide if he would raise the tariff rate above 25 percent in response to China’s depreciation

content.text: China can choose either path, but it will most likely limit near-term depreciation while it tests whether a deal is still possible.
content.reason: An actor with ample policy room keeps its strongest lever in reserve while negotiations remain possible.

passages.source_excerpt: That’s why my best guess is that China limits any near-term move as it tries to see if there is still time (and will) to cut a deal that avoids further escalation.

content.text: China's leadership weighs the risk of provoking further US escalation above the immediate export gains from a weaker yuan.
content.reason: Forecasts of policy restraint presume decision-makers value avoiding escalation over short-term gains.

content.text: Trump may not actually want a deal if he is fixated on the bilateral deficit, which a modest deal would not fix.
content.reason: A negotiator whose goal a deal cannot meet may prefer continued conflict.

passages.source_excerpt: As David Fickling notes, if Trump is fixated on the bilateral deficit, it isn’t entirely obvious that Trump really wants a deal.
